title: Scaling and normalising
story:
Scaling looks cosmetic and is not. A distance sums squared differences across columns, a regularisation penalty sums coefficients across columns, and a gradient step moves along a surface whose curvature in each direction depends on that column's spread. All three add features together, and adding requires comparable units. Leave a column in a unit that happens to produce large numbers and it will dominate the sum, not because it matters more but because of how it was recorded.

So the rule of thumb is about the method rather than the data. Anything that computes a distance, imposes a penalty on coefficients, or takes gradient steps across features is sensitive to scale. Anything that considers one feature at a time and only cares about the order of values within it is not — a tree splits on whether a value is above or below a threshold, and any transform that preserves order moves the threshold without changing the split.

The awkward part is that the numbers you scale by are themselves statistics of the data you have. Centre by the mean and divide by the standard deviation, and both the centre and the spread were estimated from the sample, including whatever is unusual in it. The documentation is blunt: if your data contains many outliers, scaling using the mean and variance of the data is likely to not work very well, and it points instead to a robust scaler as a drop-in replacement which uses more robust estimates for the center and range of your data. The mechanism is worth seeing: one extreme value inflates the estimated spread, everything divides by that inflated number, and the bulk of the data is compressed into a narrow band around zero — the outlier has not been handled, it has set the scale for everyone else.

The rank-based alternative escapes that and pays for it elsewhere. A quantile transform smooths out unusual distributions and is less influenced by outliers than scaling methods, and the same documentation immediately adds that it does, however, distort correlations and distances within and across features. Which is the trade in one sentence: replacing values by their ranks throws away how far apart they were, and how far apart they were is exactly what a distance was measuring.

The last piece is where the statistic is computed. The transformer computes the mean and standard deviation on a training set so as to later re-apply the same transformation on the testing set, which is why it is described as suitable for the early steps of a Pipeline — and the documented example annotates the scoring call as applying scaling on testing data, without leaking training data. A scale fitted on everything before splitting has carried the held-out rows' spread into the training step.

problem.name: Feature scaling
problem.shape: A method combines several features by adding them together, and the features are recorded in units that have nothing to do with one another.
tell: the method computes a distance, a penalty on coefficients, or a gradient across features
one column is in thousands and another is a proportion
the coefficient on one feature is enormous and on another is tiny
the scaling statistic was computed before the data was split
problem.move: Scale when the method sums across features and not otherwise. Estimate the centre and spread on the training portion alone and apply them to everything else, which is what a pipeline makes structural rather than remembered. Where the sample carries extreme values, use robust estimates of centre and range instead of the mean and standard deviation.
problem.invariant: Scaling is a per-feature monotone transform. It changes the relative contribution of features to anything that adds them together, and it changes nothing at all for a method that only compares values within one feature.
problem.breaks: The scaling constants are statistics of the sample, so they inherit whatever is unusual in it: one extreme value inflates the estimated spread, everything is divided by that inflated number, and the bulk of the data is compressed into a narrow band. The outlier has not been handled — it has set the scale for every other row.

cost.time: one pass to estimate the statistics and one to apply them, which is negligible beside the model
cost.space: two numbers per feature, kept as part of the fitted model because they must be reapplied at prediction time
cost.beats: leaving the units alone, which silently weights the model by how each column happened to be recorded, and rank-based transforms, which resist outliers at the cost of distorting the correlations and distances they were meant to preserve

worked.problem: You scaled the features. The linear model's score changed and the tree-based model's score did not move at all. Why?
worked.reasoning:
Because the two models use the feature values for different things, and only one of those things is affected by a monotone change of units.

A linear model sums the features, weighted. That sum is only meaningful if the terms are commensurable, and the penalty applied to the coefficients is a second place the units enter: a coefficient's size depends on the scale of its feature, so a shared penalty is not shared at all when the features have different spreads — it falls hardest on whichever column happened to be recorded in small units. Standardising makes the penalty mean the same thing in every direction, and it also makes the optimisation better conditioned, because gradient steps move along a surface whose curvature per direction reflects the spread of that feature. So scaling moves the score.

A tree does not sum anything. It considers one feature at a time and asks whether a value falls above or below a threshold, then chooses the threshold to best separate the rows. Any transform that preserves the order of values within a column preserves every possible partition of the rows — the threshold that used to be at one number is now at its image under the transform, and the same rows go the same way. Standardising is such a transform, so the fitted tree is the same tree and the score is identical rather than merely similar.

The useful generalisation is that tree-based methods are invariant to any monotone per-feature transform. That covers standardising, min-max scaling, and taking logs. It also means the rank-based transform will not help a tree either, and the effort of applying it there buys nothing.

Two qualifications I would offer. First, exact identity holds for a single deterministic tree; with a random forest or gradient boosting there is sampling and floating-point arithmetic in play, so expect identical or trivially different rather than bit-identical. Second, the invariance is per-feature and does not extend to anything that combines features — an oblique split, or a distance computed before the tree, is scale-sensitive like everything else.

So if a tree-based score moved noticeably after scaling, I would not explain it. I would look for the bug, because it should not have.

problem.practice: Fit a linear model and a tree on the same unscaled data, then again on standardised data, and compare all four scores. Then add a single extreme value to one column, standardise again, and look at what happened to the spread of the other rows in that column.

beats.broke: Distances, coefficient penalties and gradient steps all combine features by adding them together, so the unit a column happens to be recorded in decides how much of the model's attention it receives.
beats.fix: Put the columns on a comparable scale before any method that sums across them, estimating the centre and spread from the training portion alone and applying them to everything else.
beats.cost: The centre and spread are themselves statistics of the sample, so one extreme value sets the scale and compresses everything else into a narrow band — and the rank-based alternative that resists this distorts the correlations and distances it was brought in to preserve.

interview.q: You scaled the features. The linear model's score changed and the tree-based model's score did not move at all. Why?
interview.trap: Treating the unchanged score as suspicious, or concluding that scaling does not matter in general. It is the expected result: a tree splits on order within a feature, and scaling preserves order.
interview.answer:
Because the two models use the values for different purposes, and only one of those purposes notices a monotone change of units.

The linear model forms a weighted sum of the features, which is only meaningful when the terms are commensurable, and the penalty on its coefficients is a second place the units enter: a coefficient's magnitude depends on its feature's scale, so a shared penalty is not shared at all across features with different spreads — it falls hardest on whichever column was recorded in the smallest units. Standardising makes the penalty mean the same thing in every direction, and it conditions the optimisation better, since the curvature in each direction reflects that feature's spread. So the score moves.

The tree sums nothing. It takes one feature at a time and asks whether a value is above or below a threshold, choosing the threshold that best separates the rows. Any transform preserving the order of values within a column preserves every achievable partition — the threshold moves to its image under the transform and the same rows go the same way. Standardising is such a transform, so it is the same tree and the score is identical rather than close.

The generalisation is that tree-based methods are invariant to any monotone per-feature transform: standardising, min-max scaling, taking logs. It also follows that a rank-based transform buys a tree nothing.

Two qualifications. Exact identity is a statement about a single deterministic tree; with a forest or with boosting there is sampling and floating-point arithmetic involved, so expect identical or trivially different. And the invariance is per-feature — it does not extend to anything combining features, such as an oblique split or a distance computed before the model.

Which gives a useful check rather than just an explanation: if a tree-based score had moved noticeably after scaling, I would go looking for the bug, because it should not have.

takeaway: Scaling matters exactly when a method adds features together and not at all when it compares values within one, and because the constants you scale by are statistics of the sample, a single extreme value can set the scale for every other row.
